entry.evidence: no study is available covering whole Upper Ganga basin for a longer period of investigation creating a large database of water quality

sequences.source_document: Sharma et al. 2022, J. Asian Earth Sci. X 8, 100108 (PDF body; XML abstract and captions)

steps.action: The authors pose a basin-wide question about the spatial and temporal hydrochemistry of the Upper Ganga Basin and the processes controlling it, and propose to compare solute fluxes of the three rivers.
steps.quote: a comprehensive study of spatial and temporal hydro-chemical characteristics and hydrogeochemical processes controlling the hydrochemistry of Upper Ganga Basin

steps.action: They design a monitoring network: 13 sites (4 Bhagirathi, 6 Alaknanda, 3 Ganga), sampled monthly from September 2016 to May 2018, giving 273 samples.
steps.quote: Thirteen sampling sites have been selected for water quality assessment in Upper Ganga Basin and monitoring is carried out on monthly basis

steps.action: They take grab samples and measure EC and pH in the field, then measure major ions in the laboratory by ion chromatography and titration, DO/BOD by Winkler titration, and COD by closed reflux.
steps.quote: using Metrohm make Ion Chromatograph (IC) model 930 (for anions and cations)

steps.action: They check measurement quality: analytical precision (RSD < 5%) and the normalized inorganic charge balance between cations and anions (within ±5%).
steps.quote: Overall data reproducibility for cations and anions was within ± 5% indicating the high accuracy of the data.

steps.action: They test the premises of the multivariate analysis: Shapiro-Wilk and Royston normality tests, log transformation and Z-scores, a K-S test of the transformed data, and Kaiser normalization for PCA adequacy.
steps.quote: To achieve a normal like distribution, the original set of variables was transformed using a logarithmic transformation

steps.action: They report ranges and means of physicochemical parameters and major ions for each river and site, with temporal series.
steps.quote: The pH value varied from 6.3 to 8.6, 6.8 to 8.3 and 7.3 to 8.9 for rivers Bhagirathi, Alaknanda and Ganga respectively

steps.action: They compare the values with BIS, WHO and CPCB criteria limits; COD and TSS exceed the CPCB river criteria at most sites, while the ions are within limits.
steps.quote: COD values were higher than the maximum criteria limit of 10 mg/L for the river for drinking purposes prescribed by CPCB

steps.action: They compare pH, TSS seasonality, hardness, anion and cation orders with earlier Himalayan studies and find them similar.
steps.quote: This observation is quite similar to earlier results reported by

steps.action: From ionic proportions and the (Ca+Mg)/(Na+K) and (Ca+Mg)/Tz+ ratios, they infer that carbonate weathering mainly regulates the meltwater chemistry.
steps.quote: showing that hydro geochemistry of Gangotri glacier meltwater is mainly regulated by carbonate weathering

steps.action: They name rival solute sources: carbonate weathering, silicate weathering, evaporite dissolution, atmospheric input, ion exchange and anthropogenic input.
steps.quote: may be derived either from the weathering of carbonates or the dissolution of evaporates

steps.action: They take stoichiometric expectations (1:1 equivalent lines) and the Gibbs (1970) process fields as the predictions of each source.
steps.quote: Under natural conditions (Ca + Mg)/HCO3 equivalent ratio from carbonate weathering is one.

steps.action: They compare ion scatter plots with the 1:1 equilines and plot samples on Gibbs diagrams; nearly all samples fall in the rock-dominance zone.
steps.quote: almost all collected surface water samples from rivers Bhagirathi, Alaknanda and Ganga fall in rock dominance zone

steps.action: They judge atmospheric/evaporite input and silicate weathering to be minor contributors, from the low Na/Cl ratio and the low (Na+K) share of total cations.
steps.quote: negates the possible impact of atmospheric pollution on the glacier water

steps.action: They compute the C ratio (method in the supplement, not supplied) for each site and month to infer the proton source driving weathering.
steps.quote: The average C ratio for meltwater of Bhagirathi River at Gangotri and Dabrani was found at 0.254 and 0.465 respectively

steps.action: They compare C ratios with the 0.5 threshold. Bhagirathi up to Dabrani is below 0.5 (sulphide oxidation); downstream Bhagirathi, all Alaknanda and Ganga sites are above 0.5 (carbonation coupled with sulphide oxidation).
steps.quote: Here it is clearly revealed the meltwater chemistry of river Bhagirathi upto Dabrani is dominated by sulphate

steps.action: They use discharge at Devprayag (Bhagirathi, Alaknanda) and Rishikesh (Ganga), supplied by the Central Water Commission.
steps.quote: Discharge data used in the study was provided by Central Water Commission

steps.action: They fit logarithmic concentration-flow relations. Most constituents dilute with flow, with exceptions for NO3, NH4 and PO4 in the Ganga and PO4 in the Alaknanda.
steps.quote: all the constituents exhibited a dilution of concentration with the increasing flow of the river

steps.action: They compute daily solute and sediment fluxes for each river (Table S1) and plot them against the discharge time series.
steps.quote: the flux of almost all the parameters follows the same trend as that of discharge

steps.action: They regress fluxes on discharge. Correlations are high for the Bhagirathi (TDS r2 = 0.89) and low for the Alaknanda and Ganga, except PO4 in the Alaknanda.
steps.quote: The best correlation has been shown by TDS (r2 = 0.89) for the river Bhagirathi

steps.action: They use Pearson correlation matrices of 20 parameters for each river as a second analysis of solute sources (Tables S2-S4).
steps.quote: The impact of halite dissolution during summer preferably at Haridwar and Rishikesh is significantly supported by the correlation between Na and Cl.

steps.action: They run PCA with Varimax rotation for each river; five components explain 76-87% of the variance (Table 3 cumulative percentages), and they read hardness/bicarbonate and hydronium factors as support for carbonate weathering.
steps.quote: The release of H+ ions into the stream supports the phenomena of carbonate weathering occurring in the Upper Ganga Basin.

steps.action: They keep the headline claim: sulphide oxidation dominates the Bhagirathi up to Dabrani (Gangotri glacial continuum), carbonation dominates downstream to Haridwar, and carbonate dissolution dominates throughout the Alaknanda.
steps.quote: the dominance of sulphide oxidation in River Bhagirathi upto Dabrani revealing the continuum of Gangotri glacial processes followed by carbonate dissolution upto Haridwar

end.claim: Weathering in the Upper Ganga Basin is driven by sulphide oxidation and carbonation: sulphide oxidation dominates the Bhagirathi up to Dabrani (Gangotri glacial continuum), carbonate dissolution dominates downstream to Haridwar, and it dominates the whole Alaknanda.

decisive_move.sentence: The site-by-site C ratio, judged against the 0.5 threshold, is what separates the sulphide-oxidation stretch of the upper Bhagirathi from the carbonation-dominated reaches.

gates.evidence: Action: sampling followed a fixed monthly monitoring design under the NMSHE project (p. 16) and a literature gap (p. 2), not a stated hypothesis. Claim: the C ratio and the equiline diagnostics could have shown otherwise, but no formal test, uncertainty or rival-specific prediction beyond these thresholds is reported (p. 9). Registration: nothing is stated as fixed before the data.

limits:
How sources were handled:
- The XML text holds only the abstract and captions, so body steps are located by PDF page.
- The C ratio calculation and Tables S1-S4 are in a supplement that was not supplied.
- No review file was supplied, so there is no review sequence.

What the paper does not show:
- No uncertainty is given on the C ratios, fluxes or regressions.
- Discharge was available only at Devprayag and Rishikesh, so fluxes for upstream sites are not computed.
- The flux-discharge correlations (Fig. 9) are partly built in, because flux is concentration times discharge. The paper does not address this (inference).
- The text is internally inconsistent: silicate weathering is called minor (p. 8, p. 15), yet HCO3-Na-Cl correlations and the (Ca+Mg) vs HCO3+SO4 plot are attributed to silicate weathering (p. 9, p. 12).
- The conclusions call meltwater 'slightly acidic' (p. 15) while the results say 'slightly alkaline' (p. 4).
- Pearson correlation is justified by non-normality (p. 4), which is unusual.
- The exact rule for retaining five PCs is not stated (inference: eigenvalue > 1, Table 3).

Sub-claim statuses:
- Carbonate weathering dominates via cation ratios: best_explanation.
- COD and TSS exceed CPCB criteria at most sites: estimate_with_resolution (descriptive, no uncertainty).
- Dilution of concentrations with flow: regularity_in_range (range not stated, many R2 near 0).
- Flux-discharge correlation high for the Bhagirathi, low elsewhere: regularity_in_range.
- Five PCs suffice: none (descriptive).

alternatives_considered.chosen: Natural-log transformation and Z-score standardization of the 20 parameters
alternatives_considered.reason: To achieve a normal like distribution and protect dissimilarity metrics from being severely influenced
Data had a non-normal distribution and this method is best suitable for reducing deviation of variables

alternatives_considered.chosen: Varimax orthogonal rotation of retained factors
alternatives_considered.reason: Simplifies interpretation of each component (few large loadings, many near-zero loadings)
